RESPONSE BASED MODEL OF STRESS (HANS SELYE)

title: Homeostasis and the Inflammatory Response
body:
## Homeostasis
A state of dynamic equilibrium (balance, stability), maintained by **negative feedback**. Walter Cannon's concepts include the sympatho-adreno-medullary response (fight or flight), adreno-cortical response and neurohypophyseal response.

## Inflammation
A local response to tissue injury or infection that mobilises specific and non-specific defenses. Purposes: localise the injury, protect tissue from further injury, prepare tissue for repair.

## Cellular response
- **Neutrophils** arrive first.
- **Monocytes** perform phagocytosis in chronic injury.
- **Lymphocytes** handle immune responses.

## Processes
- Margination/pavementing: phagocytes line up along vessel walls.
- Emigration/diapedesis: phagocytes move out of vessels.
- Chemotaxis: injured tissue releases substances that attract phagocytes.
- Phagocytosis: phagocytes engulf antigens.

## Exudate
Fluid that escaped the vessels plus dead phagocytes and tissue cells. Fibrinogen (becoming fibrin), thromboplastin from injured cells, and platelets form a mesh that walls off the area and stops spread. When the agent is overcome, lymphatic drainage clears the exudate.

## Memory aid
Order of events: Margination, Emigration, Chemotaxis, Phagocytosis (MECP, made up).

## Related topics
[[Wound Healing: Regeneration, Scar and Intentions]], [[Stress and the General Adaptation Syndrome]]

## Check against your textbook
The handout says homeostasis is more commonly called "hemodynamics"; the usual term is homeodynamics (hemodynamics means blood flow). Verify.

title: Wound Healing: Regeneration, Scar and Intentions
body:
## What it is
Healing is the reparative phase after inflammation. Tissue is repaired by regeneration or by scar.

## Must-know facts
- **Regeneration:** damaged cells replaced by new cells identical in structure and function (works in tissues that can multiply, such as skin surface).
- **Scar formation:** damaged cells replaced by fibrous tissue.
  - Granulation tissue: early stage; pink or red, fragile, gelatinous, rich in new vessels. Healthy granulation looks beefy red; pale or dusky tissue suggests poor perfusion.
  - Cicatrix (scar): later stage; tissue shrinks as collagen fibers contract.
- **Healing by first intention:** clean-cut wound with approximated edges; minimal or no scar (surgical incision).
- **Second intention:** extensive wound with large tissue loss; edges not joined, healing from the base up; longer and more scarring (pressure ulcer).
- **Third intention:** delayed surgical closure of an infected wound; left open to drain or clean, then closed.

## Assessment
Wound edges, drainage color and amount, odor, redness, warmth, swelling, temperature, pain.

## Priority nursing actions
Prevent infection first (hand hygiene, aseptic dressing); protect and keep moist per order; support nutrition (protein, vitamin C, zinc) because healing needs building materials.

## Complications and red flags
Infection (fever, pus, spreading redness), dehiscence (edges separate), evisceration (organs protrude), delayed healing in diabetes, poor nutrition or poor circulation.

## Client teaching
Keep the dressing clean and dry, report fever or discharge, eat protein, stop smoking.

## How the exam asks about it
Match the wound: sutured clean incision = first; large open ulcer = second; contaminated wound closed after several days = third. Beefy red granulation is a good sign.

## Related topics
[[Homeostasis and the Inflammatory Response]], [[Cellular Events of Inflammation: Margination to Phagocytosis]], [[Pressure Ulcer Risk Factors and Stages]]

## Check against your textbook
Dehiscence, evisceration and nutrition details are standard teaching I added, not in the handout.

title: Body Temperature: Heat Loss, Fever and Hypothermia
body:
## What it is
Temperature is the balance between heat produced and heat lost. Vital (cardinal) signs: temperature, pulse, respirations, blood pressure, plus pain as the fifth.

## Types
- **Core:** deep tissues (abdominal and pelvic cavity).
- **Surface:** skin, subcutaneous tissue and fat; rises and falls with the environment.

## Heat loss
- Radiation: surface to surface without contact.
- Conduction: direct contact.
- Convection: air currents.
- Evaporation: moisture vaporising from respiratory tract, mouth and skin.

## Factors affecting temperature
Age, circadian rhythm (highest about 4-6 pm, lowest about 4-6 am), exercise, hormones (progesterone raises it), stress, environment.

## Alterations
- **Pyrexia/fever:** above usual range. **Hyperpyrexia:** 41 C (105.8 F) and above.
- **Hypothermia:** core temperature below normal; from excess heat loss, poor heat production or impaired hypothalamic regulation.

## Fever patterns
- Intermittent: alternates regularly between fever and normal/subnormal.
- Remittent: wide fluctuations (over 2 C in 24 h), always above normal.
- Relapsing: a few febrile days then 1-2 normal days.
- Constant: minimal change, stays above normal.
- Spike: rapid rise then return to normal within hours.

## Related topics
[[Measuring Temperature by Site and Converting Scales]], [[Tepid Sponge Bath for Fever]], [[Pulse Assessment: Sites and Characteristics]]

title: Measuring Temperature by Site and Converting Scales
body:
## Oral
Most convenient. Wait 30 minutes after hot/cold drinks, food or smoking. Avoid in oral lesions or surgery, dyspnea, cough, vomiting, oronasal pack, NGT or ET tube, seizure-prone, very young, unconscious, restless or confused clients. Place the bulb beside the frenulum for 2-3 minutes. Normal 36-37.5 C.

## Rectal
Very accurate. Avoid with anal/rectal conditions or surgery, diarrhea, quadriplegia and myocardial infarction. Use gloves, Sim's (lateral) position, lubricate, ask the client to breathe slowly, never force. Hold 2 minutes. Normal 36-37.8 C.

## Axillary
Safest and non-invasive. Pat the axilla dry (rubbing raises skin temperature), bulb in the center, arm tight across chest, leave about 9 minutes.

## Tympanic
Common estimate of core temperature. Adults: pull pinna back and up. Children under 3: pull straight back and slightly down. Over 3: back and up. Aim toward the eardrum, insert snugly with a circular motion.

## Conversions
- F to C: 5/9 x (F - 32)
- C to F: (C x 9/5) + 32

## Exam reasoning
Pick the site that is safe for the client's condition: axillary for the very young or confused, not oral.

## Related topics
[[Body Temperature: Heat Loss, Fever and Hypothermia]], [[Tepid Sponge Bath for Fever]]

## Check against your textbook
The handout gives rectal insertion as 15 cm (6 in) in adults and 11 cm in children; standard texts say about 3-4 cm (1.5 in) for adults. Axillary time of 9 minutes and the quoted normal ranges should also be verified.

title: Tepid Sponge Bath for Fever
body:
## What it is
A cooling measure using lukewarm water to bring down a raised temperature by evaporation and conduction.

## Must-know facts
- Start when body temperature rises 1-2 C.
- Water temperature in the handout: 32 C (tepid, not cold).
- Apply by **patting** (not rubbing). Rationale: friction creates heat and raises skin temperature.
- Do **not** use alcohol. Rationale: it dries and irritates the skin.
- Heat loss route it uses: evaporation and conduction.

## Assessment
Temperature before and after (30 minutes), pulse, skin color, comfort, hydration, mental status.

## Priority nursing actions
Check vital signs first, then give privacy and cover the body part not being sponged. Stop if the client shivers (shivering makes heat), becomes pale, bluish or uncomfortable. Offer fluids. Treat the cause and give antipyretics as ordered.

## Complications and red flags
Shivering, chilling, very high fever with confusion or seizure: report at once.

## Client teaching
Explain why the bath is gentle and why alcohol is avoided; keep fluids up and wear light clothing.

## How the exam asks about it
The trap is the choice with alcohol, ice-cold water or vigorous rubbing; reject it. Water should be tepid, applied by patting.

## Related topics
[[Body Temperature: Heat Loss, Fever and Hypothermia]], [[Types of Fever and Factors Affecting Body Temperature]], [[Bed Bath Guidelines]]

## Check against your textbook
The handout gives only the start criterion, 32 C, patting and no alcohol; the shivering advice is standard teaching I added.

title: Pulse Assessment: Sites and Characteristics
body:
## What it is
The pulse is the wave of blood created by left ventricular contraction. Cardiac output = stroke volume x heart rate; normal about 5 L per minute.

## Factors affecting pulse
Age, gender (male lower than female), exercise, fever, medications, hypovolemia, stress, position change, pathology.

## Pulse sites and uses
- Temporal: when radial is not accessible.
- Carotid: cardiac arrest (adults).
- Radial: readily accessible, routine.
- Apical: routine for infants and children up to 3 years.
- Brachial: BP measurement; cardiac arrest in infants.
- Femoral: cardiac arrest/shock, leg circulation.
- Popliteal: lower leg circulation.
- Posterior tibial and dorsalis pedis: circulation to the foot.

## What to assess
- Rate: adult 60-100/min; tachycardia over 100; bradycardia under 60.
- Rhythm: irregular = dysrhythmia/arrhythmia.
- Volume: normal felt with moderate pressure; full bounding is hard to obliterate; weak/thready is easily obliterated.
- Arterial wall: straight, smooth, soft, pliable.
- **Pulse deficit:** difference between apical and radial rates.
- Scale: 0 absent, 1+ weak/thready, 2+ normal, 3+ bounding.

## Related topics
[[Respiration Assessment and Abnormal Breathing Terms]], [[Blood Pressure: Determinants, Classification and Measurement]], [[Body Temperature: Heat Loss, Fever and Hypothermia]]

title: Respiration Assessment and Abnormal Breathing Terms
body:
## Three processes
- **Ventilation:** air moving in and out (inhalation, exhalation).
- **Diffusion:** gas exchange from higher to lower pressure at the alveolocapillary membrane.
- **Perfusion:** blood available to carry gases, nutrients and wastes.

## Control and types
- Costal (thoracic) breathing uses intercostal and accessory muscles; diaphragmatic (abdominal) uses the diaphragm.
- Medulla oblongata is the primary respiratory center; CO2 is the main chemical stimulus.
- Pons: pneumotaxic center (rhythm) and apneustic center (deep prolonged inspiration).
- Carotid and aortic bodies: chemoreceptors sensitive to O2 and CO2.

## Assessment
Normal rate 12-20/min; note depth (normal, deep, shallow), rhythm, and quality/effort and sound. Rate is affected by exercise, stress, environment, altitude and medications.

## Terms
- Tachypnea: fast shallow (over 20). Bradypnea: slow (under 12). Apnea: none.
- Hyperventilation: rapid deep. Hypoventilation: shallow.
- Cheyne-Stokes: deep to shallow then apnea. Kussmaul: rapid, deep, labored. Biot: shallow breaths interrupted by apnea.
- Dyspnea: difficult breathing. Orthopnea: breathes only when upright.
- Stridor: harsh high sound on inspiration. Stertor: snoring. Wheeze: high musical sound on expiration. Bubbling: gurgling through secretions.

## Related topics
[[Pulse Assessment: Sites and Characteristics]], [[Respiratory Failure Recognition]], [[Airway Obstruction and Choking]]

## Check against your textbook
The handout defines tachypnea as "quick, shallow"; hyperventilation as rapid and deep. Confirm definitions with your text.

title: Blood Pressure: Determinants, Classification and Measurement
body:
## Definitions
BP is pressure of blood against arterial walls. Systolic = ventricular contraction; diastolic = ventricles at rest; pulse pressure = systolic minus diastolic. Hypertension is persistently high; hypotension low; orthostatic hypotension is a drop on sitting or standing.

## Determinants
Pumping action of the heart (weak = lower BP), peripheral vascular resistance, vessel diameter (vasoconstriction raises BP), blood volume (loss lowers BP), blood viscosity (thicker raises BP).

## Other factors
Age, gender, exercise, medications, stress, obesity, race, diurnal variation, disease.

## Classification (handout)
- Normal: under 120 and under 80
- Prehypertension: 120-139 or 80-89
- Stage 1: 140-159 or 90-99
- Stage 2: 160 or more, or 100 or more

## Korotkoff sounds
Phase 1 first faint tapping; 2 swishing; 3 crisper, louder; 4 muffled blowing; 5 silence.

## Technique
Correct cuff size; client rested (wait 30 minutes after exercise, smoking, caffeine); arm at heart level, supported; cuff 1 inch above the antecubital space; palpate first, then auscultate; inflate 30 mmHg above where the pulse disappeared; deflate 2-3 mmHg per second; wait 1-2 minutes before repeating.

## Errors
- False **low**: cuff bladder too wide; arm above heart level.
- False **high**: cuff too narrow or loose; arm below heart level or unsupported; insufficient rest.

## Related topics
[[Pulse Assessment: Sites and Characteristics]], [[Pain Assessment: Types, PQRST and Scales]]

## Check against your textbook
The handout's stage 2 reads ">160 or >100"; current guidance usually uses 160 or above. The classification system (older JNC 7) may differ from your textbook.

title: Pain Assessment: Types, PQRST and Scales
body:
## What it is
Pain is an unpleasant sensory and emotional experience tied to actual or potential tissue damage. It is called the fifth vital sign (American Pain Society, 2003). The client's own report is the most reliable measure.

## Must-know facts
- Acute: seconds up to 6 months. Chronic: constant or intermittent, 6 months or longer (persistent non-malignant). Cancer-related pain is a third group.
- PQRST: **P**rovoking factors (what were you doing when it began), **Q**uality (throbbing, burning, aching, stabbing), **R**adiation (where; elsewhere; referred pain spreads to another area), **S**everity (0 to 10 scale; mild to severe), **T**ime (onset and duration; acute or chronic).
- Scales: descriptive intensity (no pain to worst possible), numeric 0-10, visual analogue (line from no pain to as bad as it could be), Faces scale (suitable for children).

## Assessment
Ask about location, character, intensity, what helps, what worsens, and effect on sleep, appetite and activity. Watch behavior (grimace, guarding, vital-sign changes) when the client cannot speak.

## Priority nursing actions
Assess before treating; give analgesic as ordered and reassess after it should have worked. For sudden severe chest or abdominal pain, assess ABC and vital signs and call for help first.

## Complications and red flags
New severe pain, pain with changes in vital signs, or pain not relieved by treatment: report.

## Client teaching
Report pain early, use the same scale each time, do not wait until pain is severe.

## How the exam asks about it
Pick the best first action (assess pain with a scale) and the right tool for a child (Faces). Subjective report outranks vital signs.

## Related topics
[[NSAIDs: COX-1 and COX-2 Inhibitors]], [[Blood Pressure: Determinants, Classification and Measurement]]

title: Physical Examination: Techniques, Sequence and Privacy
body:
## General rules
- Head-to-toe (cephalocaudal). Check the client's level of awareness first.
- Most important consideration: prepare the client physically and psychologically.
- Protect privacy; get equipment ready beforehand.

## Techniques (IPPA)
Inspection (sight), Palpation (touch with finger pads), Percussion (tapping to produce sound), Auscultation (stethoscope). Light palpation precedes deep palpation.

## Abdomen: IAPePa
Inspection, Auscultation, Percussion, Palpation. Auscultate before touching so bowel sounds are not altered.

## Special considerations
- Palpate the painful quadrant last.
- No abdominal palpation if tumor of the liver or kidneys.
- Flex the knees to relax abdominal muscles.
- Quadrant order in the handout: right lower, right upper, left upper, left lower.
- Best position for the chest: sitting upright; for the back: standing.
- Palpate neck nodes or thyroid from behind the client.
- Darken the room for ophthalmoscopy.
- A male examiner with a female client needs a female attendant.

## Related topics
[[Percussion Sounds and Normal Breath Sounds]], [[Examination Positions]]

## Check against your textbook
Verify the quadrant sequence; many texts start in the right lower quadrant and move clockwise, which matches the handout.

title: Percussion Sounds and Normal Breath Sounds
body:
## What it is
Percussion is tapping the body to produce sound; auscultation is listening with a stethoscope. Together they locate solid, fluid and air.

## Must-know facts
Percussion sounds, from soft to loud:
- Flatness: soft, extremely dull; muscle and bone (also large pleural effusion).
- Dullness: medium, thud-like; liver and heart.
- Resonance: loud, hollow; normal lung.
- Hyperresonance: very loud, booming; emphysematous lung (air trapping).
- Tympany: loud, musical; stomach or bowel filled with gas.

Normal breath sounds:
- Vesicular: soft, low-pitched "gentle sighing" over small airways (bronchioles and alveoli); heard over most of the lung periphery.
- Bronchovesicular: moderate pitch and intensity, "blowing", over larger bronchi.
- Bronchial (tubular): high-pitched, loud, harsh, over the trachea.

## Assessment
Listen over each lung field and compare side to side (symmetry) on a bare chest; sitting upright is best for the chest.

## Priority nursing actions
Report sounds in the wrong place (bronchial sounds over the lung periphery can mean consolidation) and absent sounds (possible collapse).

## How the exam asks about it
Match sound to place: hyperresonance = emphysema, tympany = gas-filled stomach, dullness = liver. Hyperresonant percussion plus absent sounds can suggest pneumothorax.

## Memory aid
Going from solid to air: flat, dull, resonant, hyperresonant, tympanic.

## Related topics
[[Physical Examination: Techniques, Sequence and Privacy]], [[Respiration Assessment and Abnormal Breathing Terms]], [[Abdominal and Regional Examination: Sequence and Special Rules]]

## Check against your textbook
Pneumothorax and consolidation links are standard teaching I added, not in the handout.

title: Examination Positions
body:
## What it is
Body positions used for examination, each chosen to expose a particular area and keep the client comfortable and covered.

## Must-know facts
- **Dorsal recumbent:** on the back, knees flexed, hips externally rotated; used for head and neck, axillae, anterior chest, lungs, breasts, heart, abdomen, extremities, peripheral pulses, vital signs and vagina.
- **Dorsal (supine):** on the back, legs extended; head and neck, axillae, front chest, lungs, breasts, heart, extremities, pulses.
- **Sitting:** upright, back unsupported, legs hanging; head and neck, axillae, front and back chest, lungs, breasts, heart, vital signs, arms and legs, reflexes.
- **Lithotomy:** on the back with feet in stirrups, hips at table edge; female genitals, rectum and reproductive tract.
- **Sim's:** lying on the side, lower arm behind, upper leg flexed; rectum and vagina (also rectal temperature, enema).
- **Prone:** face down; posterior thorax and hips.

## Priority nursing actions
Drape so only the area under examination is exposed. Lithotomy is tiring and exposes the client: keep it short, explain, and change position slowly to avoid dizziness. Flex knees for abdominal examination.

## Complications and red flags
Dizziness on rising, back strain, embarrassment; clients with breathing problems may need a higher head position.

## How the exam asks about it
Match position to procedure: Pap smear = lithotomy; rectal examination or enema = Sim's; back exam = sitting or prone.

## Memory aid
Sim's = side; Lithotomy = Legs in stirrups.

## Related topics
[[Physical Examination: Techniques, Sequence and Privacy]], [[Abdominal and Regional Examination: Sequence and Special Rules]], [[Measuring Temperature by Site and Converting Scales]]

## Check against your textbook
Reflexes, Pap smear and enema examples include standard teaching I added beyond the handout.

title: Common Skin Problems and Skin Lesion Types
body:
## Common skin problems
- Abrasion: superficial layers scraped away; red or weeping; keep clean and dry.
- Excessive dryness: scaly, rough; increase oral fluids, moisturise, avoid alcohol.
- Acne: inflammation around sebaceous glands; avoid high-fat foods, reduce stress, do not squeeze pimples.
- Erythema: redness (rash, sun, fever); wash well, antiseptic lotion for itching.
- Hyperhidrosis: excessive sweating. Bromhidrosis: foul-smelling sweat.
- Vitiligo: hypopigmented patches from loss of melanocytes.

## Primary lesions
- Macule: flat, under 1 cm (freckle). Patch: over 1 cm (port-wine mark).
- Papule: raised, under 0.5 cm (nevus, acne). Plaque: larger than a papule.
- Nodule: solid mass into the dermis. Tumor: larger than a nodule.
- Vesicle: fluid-filled, under 1 cm (chickenpox). Bulla: large fluid-filled sac.
- Pustule: filled with pus. Wheal: localised edema. Cyst: thick-walled, fluid or semisolid.
- Telangiectasia: dilated capillaries. Petechiae: pinpoint red spots.

## Secondary lesions
Scale, crust (dried serum or pus), erosion (epidermis lost), excoriation (scratch), atrophy (thinned skin), scar, ulcer (excavation into dermis or deeper).

## Related topics
[[Pressure Ulcer Risk Factors and Stages]], [[Bed Bath Guidelines]]

## Check against your textbook
Size cut-offs differ between textbooks (for example vesicle 0.5 vs 1 cm, plaque 0.5 vs 1 cm).

title: Bed Bath Guidelines
body:
## Purposes
Remove microorganisms, secretions and dead skin; improve circulation; promote relaxation, comfort and self-esteem; prevent odor; assess skin and body; provide activity and exercise.

## Guidelines
- Explain, provide privacy, turn off fans or air conditioning to prevent chilling.
- Offer toileting first; bed flat if allowed; client to one side.
- Cover with a bath blanket; use a bath mitt.
- Warm water, about 110-115 F (43-46 C); test with the inner wrist or elbow area and change when cooled.
- Order: eyes, face, ears, neck; far arm; near arm; hands; chest and abdomen; far leg; near leg; feet; back and buttocks; perineum last.
- Wash, rinse and dry one part at a time; rinse soap well; apply lotion; change gown and linen; clean equipment; document.

## Special points
- Eyes: clean with water only, inner to outer canthus, a separate part of the mitt for each eye.
- Limbs: long firm strokes from **distal to proximal** to promote venous return.

## Why this order
Cleanest areas first and perineum last prevents spreading microorganisms.

## Related topics
[[Tepid Sponge Bath for Fever]], [[Pressure Ulcer Prevention and Treatment]]

## Check against your textbook
The handout uses "dorsal part of the hand or elbow" for water testing; many texts say inner wrist.
outlineRefs: Considerations when bathing a client in bed

title: Pressure Ulcer Risk Factors and Stages
body:
## What it is
A lesion caused by unrelieved pressure that damages underlying tissue. Pressure over bony prominences cuts blood flow, so tissue dies.

## Must-know facts
Risk factors: friction and shearing, immobility, inadequate nutrition, fecal and urinary incontinence, decreased mental status, diminished sensation, excessive body heat, advanced age, chronic medical conditions.
Stages:
- **Stage I:** non-blanchable erythema of intact skin (stays red when pressed).
- **Stage II:** partial-thickness loss involving epidermis and possibly dermis: abrasion, blister or shallow crater.
- **Stage III:** full-thickness loss with damage or necrosis of subcutaneous tissue, may reach but not through fascia; deep crater.
- **Stage IV:** full-thickness loss with extensive destruction, necrosis, or damage to muscle, bone, tendon or joint capsule.

## Assessment
Inspect bony prominences (sacrum, heels, hips, elbows, back of head) each shift; use a risk tool (such as Braden); check the skin when turning.

## Priority nursing actions
Relieve pressure first (reposition, pressure-relieving surface), keep skin clean and dry, then nutrition and fluids. A Stage I area is the best time to act.

## Complications and red flags
Infection, osteomyelitis, sepsis; foul odor, drainage, fever.

## Client teaching
Shift weight often, keep skin dry, report red spots that do not fade.

## How the exam asks about it
Stage by the deepest tissue seen: intact red = I, blister or shallow = II, fat = III, muscle or bone = IV. Do not massage reddened bony areas.

## Related topics
[[Pressure Ulcer Prevention and Treatment]], [[Preventing Pressure Ulcers: Nutrition, Fluids, Skin and Positioning]], [[Wound Healing: Regeneration, Scar and Intentions]]

## Check against your textbook
Braden scale, sites and massage advice are standard teaching I added; black eschar cannot be staged until removed.

title: Pressure Ulcer Prevention and Treatment
body:
## Prevention
- Balanced nutrition with enough protein and vitamins A, B, C and zinc; at least 2500 ml fluids a day unless contraindicated.
- Smooth, firm, wrinkle-free bed surface.
- Keep head of bed no higher than 30 degrees to reduce shearing.
- No baby powder or cornstarch; moisturise dry skin; use alcohol-free barrier films or transparent dressings.
- No massage over bony prominences.
- Reposition every 15 minutes to 2 hours depending on risk (handout range).
- Lift with a trapeze or devices rather than dragging.
- Keep skin clean and dry; assess regularly for early signs.

## Treatment
- Minimise pressure on the ulcer.
- Clean with each dressing change (hydrocolloid dressings in the handout); use surgical asepsis.
- Send drainage for culture and sensitivity.
- Cleanse gently with alcohol-free cleanser; do not use hydrogen peroxide.
- Black (necrotic) wounds need debridement:
  - sharp: scalpel
  - mechanical: moist-to-moist dressing
  - chemical: collagenase enzymes
  - autolytic: moisture-retaining dressings

## Exam reasoning
Relieve pressure first. Early prevention beats treatment.

## Related topics
[[Pressure Ulcer Risk Factors and Stages]], [[Bed Bath Guidelines]]

## Check against your textbook
The 2-hour turning interval and exact fluid and dressing choices should be checked; mechanical debridement is usually wet-to-dry.

title: Medication Administration: Ten Rights and Drug Orders
body:
## Before giving a drug
Know dose, route, actions, expected effect, interactions and adverse effects; follow agency procedure; check the order is complete (client name, date, drug, dose, route, time, signature); compare it with the medication administration record (MAR); discuss the drug with the client and recheck the order if the client disagrees.

## Ten rights
Right drug, dose, client, route, time, documentation, approach, right to know about the drug, right to refuse, right drug history.

## Routes
Oral (absorbed in the GI tract), topical (skin or mucosa), parenteral (injection); also eye, ear and suppository. Schedules: regular, one-time, as needed.

## Essential parts of a drug order
Full name of client, date and time written, drug name, dose, frequency, route, signature of the writer.

## Drug effects
- Therapeutic: intended effect.
- Side effect: secondary, predictable, may be harmless or harmful.
- Adverse: severe, may require stopping the drug.
- Toxic: overdose or buildup from impaired metabolism or excretion.
- Idiosyncratic: unexpected, individual.
- Allergic: immunologic.

## Exam reasoning
Verify the order and the client identity first; when something looks wrong, hold the drug and clarify.

## Related topics
[[Nursing Reports and Telephone Orders]], [[Rules for Charting and Recording]]

## Check against your textbook
The handout section on types of medication orders is empty in this slice; the usual five rights are expanded here to ten as listed.

title: Nightingale's Environment Theory and Henderson's 14 Needs
body:
## What it is
Two early nursing models that the exam loves to match with a name. Nightingale looks at the surroundings of the sick person; Henderson looks at the basic human needs a nurse helps the client meet.

## Must-know facts
- **Florence Nightingale (1820-1910):** called the first nursing theorist and "Nursing with a Lamp". Environmental Theory: nursing uses the client's environment to help recovery.
- Her five environmental factors: pure fresh air, pure water, efficient drainage, cleanliness, and light (direct sunlight). A shortfall in any one produces ill health.
- She also stressed keeping the client warm, keeping noise down, and watching the diet.
- **Virginia Henderson:** the Nature of Nursing model. The nurse helps a sick or well person gain independence in doing what they would do alone if they had the strength, will or knowledge, and does it so independence returns as fast as possible.
- Henderson's 14 fundamental needs, in order: breathe normally; eat and drink adequately; eliminate body wastes; move and keep a good position; sleep and rest; select suitable clothes; maintain body temperature; keep clean and well groomed; avoid dangers and avoid injuring others; communicate with others; worship according to one's faith; work so as to feel accomplishment; take part in recreation; learn, discover or satisfy curiosity that leads to normal development and health.
- **Faye Abdellah:** Patient-Centered Approaches; lists 21 nursing problems; nursing is an art and a science serving individuals and families.

## Priority nursing actions
- Use the first 3-4 of Henderson's needs (breathing, eating, eliminating, moving) as the physiological base: this lines up with Maslow, where oxygen and basic body needs come first.
- Environmental fixes (clean, quiet, warm, safe room) are low-risk actions the nurse can do at once.

## How the exam asks about it
- "Five environmental factors" or "first nursing theorist" -> Nightingale.
- "Independence in 14 needs" -> Henderson.
- "21 nursing problems" -> Abdellah.

## Memory aid
Nightingale = the five "environment" items: air, water, drainage, cleanliness, light (think a clean, bright ward).

## Related topics
[[Definitions of Nursing and Early Nursing Theorists]], [[Nursing Theories: Johnson, King, Leininger and Levine]], [[Roles and Functions of the Nurse]]

## Check against your textbook
Wording of the 14 needs differs slightly between books; the count is what is tested.

title: Nursing Theorist Matching Sheet: Who Said What
body:
## What it is
One quick-match list of every theorist and key phrase in the handout, for the "match the theorist" question type.

## Must-know facts
- Nightingale: Environmental; 5 factors (air, water, drainage, cleanliness, light).
- Henderson: Nature of Nursing; 14 needs; independence.
- Abdellah: Patient-Centered Approaches; 21 problems.
- Johnson: Behavioral System Model; 7 subsystems (ingestive, eliminative, affiliative, aggressive, dependence, achievement, sexual and role identity).
- King: Goal Attainment; 3 systems: personal/operational (individual), interpersonal (nurse-client), social (health care system).
- Leininger: Transcultural; 3 modes: culture care preservation/maintenance, accommodation/negotiation, restructuring/repatterning.
- Levine: 4 Conservation Principles: energy, structural integrity, personal integrity, social integrity.
- Neuman: Health Care Systems Model; stressors are intrapersonal, interpersonal, extrapersonal; keep system stability.
- Orem: Self-care deficit; systems wholly compensatory, partly compensatory, supportive-educative.
- Peplau: interpersonal relations; phases orientation, identification, exploitation, resolution.
- Rogers: Science of Unitary Human Beings; irreducible energy field; whole is more than the sum of parts.
- Roy: Adaptation Model; modes physiologic, self-concept, role function, interdependence.
- Hall: Care, Core, Cure.
- Orlando: Dynamic Nurse-Patient Relationship; client behavior, nurse reaction, nurse action.
- Watson: Human Caring; 10 curative (carative) factors.
- Parse: Human Becoming; 3 assumptions.

## How to reason about it
Look for the number or the triad in the stem (3 systems, 4 principles, 7 subsystems) and match it to the theorist before reading the choices. The trap: Johnson's "ingestive" is spelled "injective" in the handout text, and "aggressive" and "affiliative" are easy to swap.

## Memory aid
Roy = "Role" (ROY has R for role function and adaptation). Orem = "Of Reliance on self-care" (self-care deficit).

## Related topics
[[Nursing Theories: Johnson, King, Leininger and Levine]], [[Nursing Theories: Neuman, Orem, Peplau and Rogers]], [[Nursing Theories: Roy, Hall, Orlando, Watson and Parse]], [[Nightingale's Environment Theory and Henderson's 14 Needs]]

## Check against your textbook
Johnson's first subsystem is usually called ingestive; the handout spells it "injective", so confirm the term.

title: Watson's 10 Caring Factors and Parse's Assumptions
body:
## What it is
Jean Watson's Human Caring Theory (1979) says caring is central to nursing and is what unifies practice. Rosemarie Parse's Human Becoming Theory is a different, more philosophical view of the person.

## Must-know facts
Watson's 10 factors, in own words:
1. Build a humanistic, altruistic value system.
2. Instill faith and hope.
3. Grow sensitivity to oneself and others.
4. Develop a helping, trusting relationship.
5. Allow and accept expression of both positive and negative feelings.
6. Use the scientific problem-solving method systematically for decisions.
7. Promote transpersonal (shared) teaching and learning.
8. Provide a supportive, protective or corrective mental, physical, social and spiritual environment.
9. Help with gratification of human needs.
10. Allow for existential-phenomenological and spiritual forces.

Parse's 3 assumptions about human becoming:
- Freely choosing personal meaning in situations.
- Co-creating rhythmic patterns of relating with the universe.
- Contranscending with emerging possibilities, with the person choosing and bearing responsibility for patterns of personal health.

## Priority nursing actions
- Factor 5 explains why the nurse first lets a distressed client express feelings (therapeutic communication) before teaching.
- Factor 6 is the nursing process itself.

## How the exam asks about it
"Which theorist stresses caring as the central focus?" -> Watson. "Human becoming" -> Parse. A stem describing "accepting expression of positive and negative feelings" maps to a carative factor.

## Related topics
[[Nursing Theories: Roy, Hall, Orlando, Watson and Parse]], [[Nursing Theorist Matching Sheet: Who Said What]], [[Communication Process and Characteristics in Nursing]]

## Check against your textbook
Watson's factors are often reworded as "caritas processes"; the number (10) is the stable fact.

title: Four Areas of Nursing Scope: Promote, Prevent, Restore, Care for the Dying
body:
## What it is
The handout divides the scope of nursing practice into four broad purposes. A question may give an activity and ask which area it belongs to.

## Must-know facts
- **Promoting health and wellness:** activities that raise quality of life and personal potential: better nutrition and fitness, preventing drug and alcohol misuse, restricting smoking, preventing accidents at home and work.
- **Preventing illness:** keep optimal health by stopping disease before it starts: immunization, prenatal and infant care, prevention of sexually transmitted infection.
- **Restoring health:** care of the ill from early detection through recovery: direct care, diagnostic and assessment procedures, teaching about recovery, rehabilitation to the best functional level.
- **Caring for the dying:** comfort and care for people of any age who are dying; help them live as comfortably as possible until death; support the people close to them in coping.

## How to reason about it
Ask: is the person well, at risk, ill, or dying? Well -> promote; at risk -> prevent; ill -> restore; dying -> comfort. The trap is immunization (prevention, not promotion) and teaching a healthy diet (promotion).

## How the exam asks about it
Short "which is an example of illness prevention" items. Rehabilitation always sits under restoring health.

## Related topics
[[Scope and Standards of Nursing Practice]], [[Leavell and Clark Prevention Levels with Examples]], [[Caring for the Dying Client and the Family]]

title: ANA Standards of Nursing Practice: The Full List
body:
## What it is
Fifteen professional standards in the handout. The first six follow the nursing process; the rest describe professional behaviour.

## Must-know facts
Practice standards (nursing-process based):
- Assessment: collect data about the client's health or situation.
- Diagnosis: analyze the data to decide the diagnosis or issue.
- Outcome identification: set expected outcomes individualized to the client.
- Planning: create a plan with strategies and alternatives.
- Implementation: carry out the plan.
- Evaluation: judge progress toward outcomes.

Professional performance standards:
- Quality of practice: keep improving quality and effectiveness.
- Education: gain and keep current knowledge and competence.
- Professional practice evaluation: judge your own practice against standards, laws and rules.
- Collegiality: contribute to peers' professional growth.
- Collaboration: work with clients, family and others.
- Ethics: build ethical provisions into all practice.
- Research: use research findings in practice.
- Resource utilization: weigh safety, effectiveness, cost and impact when planning care.
- Leadership: lead in the practice setting and the profession.

## How the exam asks about it
Give a behaviour (joins a journal club, reads new guideline, helps a new nurse) and ask which standard. Peer support -> collegiality; using studies -> research; choosing a cheaper but equally safe supply -> resource utilization.

## Memory aid
First six = ADOPIE-like: Assess, Diagnose, Outcomes, Plan, Implement, Evaluate.

## Related topics
[[Scope and Standards of Nursing Practice]], [[The Nursing Process: Purposes and Characteristics]], [[Roles and Functions of the Nurse]]

title: Source-Oriented and Problem-Oriented Records, SOAPIE and Kardex
body:
## What it is
The record-keeping formats listed in the handout and how they differ.

## Must-know facts
- **Source-oriented (traditional) record, SOMR:** each person or department writes in its own section of the chart; easy to find one discipline's information. Parts include admission sheet, face sheet, history and physical, diagnostic findings, TPR graphic sheet, doctor's order and treatment sheet, therapeutic sheet, special flow sheet, medication record, nurses' notes, discharge plan and referral summary, initial nursing assessment.
- **Problem-oriented record, POMR:** all data on a problem are brought together from every team member. Four parts:
  1. Database: everything from admission: nursing assessment, physician history, social and family data, exam results.
  2. Problem list: all aspects needing care; kept at the front of the chart; listed in the order identified; updated as problems appear or resolve.
  3. Initial list of orders or plan of care: written for the active problems by the person who listed the problem.
  4. Progress notes: narrative notes in SOAP, SOAPIE or SOAPIER form.
- **Kardex:** a quick-reference card file summarizing each client's care so the whole team can see it fast; flip cards in a portable file; may be written in pencil because details change often.

## SOAPIE pieces
S subjective data, O objective data, A assessment, P plan, I intervention, E evaluation, R revision (the extra letter in SOAPIER).

## How the exam asks about it
"Where are problems listed?" -> the problem list at the front of a POMR. "Which record is written in pencil?" -> Kardex. A client's statement of pain is subjective; a measured blood pressure is objective.

## Memory aid
SOMR = by Source (department); POMR = by Problem.

## Related topics
[[Documentation Purposes and Types of Records]], [[Rules for Charting and Recording]], [[Nursing Reports and Telephone Orders]]

title: Charting Corrections, Omitted Care and Facts Versus Opinions
body:
## What it is
The part of documentation where nurses lose marks: how to fix an error, what to do when care is not given, and how to word entries.

## Must-know facts
- Facts and observations, not opinions. Example from the handout: "Client refused medication" is fact; "Client was uncooperative" is opinion.
- Fixing a mistake: draw a single line through it, write "mistaken entry" (avoid the word "error") near it with your initials or name. Never erase, blot out or use correction fluid.
- Write on every line, not between lines; draw a line through a blank gap and sign.
- Do not chart care before it is given; document as soon as possible after assessment or intervention.
- If care is left out because the client refused, record what was omitted, why, and who was notified.
- Use dark permanent ink, approved abbreviations, correct spelling, date and time (24-hour clock avoids am/pm confusion), and sign with name and title.
- Put the client's name on every page.
- Record only information about the client's health care; irrelevant details can invade privacy.
- Only staff involved in care may read the chart.

## Priority nursing actions
Safety first, then record: give care, then chart it truthfully. Charting ahead is falsification.

## How the exam asks about it
Choose the correct way to fix a wrong entry (single line, label, initial) or the best-worded entry (objective, specific).

## Related topics
[[Rules for Charting and Recording]], [[Documentation Purposes and Types of Records]], [[Source-Oriented and Problem-Oriented Records, SOAPIE and Kardex]]

title: Interviewing in Assessment: Directive, Non-directive and Stages
body:
## What it is
An interview is planned communication with a purpose. It is one of two main data-collection methods (the other is observation).

## Must-know facts
- **Directive interview:** structured, closed (yes/no) questions, nurse sets purpose and controls pace; used when specific data are needed and in emergencies.
- **Non-directive (rapport-building) interview:** client controls subject and pacing; more open-ended questions; lets the client explain in their own words.
- **Stages:**
  - Opening: most important; build rapport and orient the client.
  - Body: client says what they think, feel and perceive in answer to questions.
  - Closing: ends the interview, summarize and thank.
- Observation has two parts: noticing the data, then selecting, organizing and interpreting it.
- Sources of data: the client (primary); support people, family, friends, caregivers, records, other professionals, lab results and literature (secondary).

## Priority nursing actions
- Emergency or unstable client: directive, brief, ABC-focused questions first (safety before rapport).
- Stable client: start open-ended to build trust, then use closed questions to fill gaps.

## How the exam asks about it
"A nurse asks, 'Do you have chest pain?'" -> directive/closed. "Tell me what brought you here" -> non-directive/open. Primary source is the client unless the client cannot speak.

## Related topics
[[Nursing Process Phase 1: Assessment Methods and Types]], [[Communication Process and Characteristics in Nursing]], [[Nursing Process Phase 2: Nursing Diagnosis]]

title: Four Types of Assessment and Data Handling
body:
## What it is
Assessment is the first nursing process phase: systematic, continuous collection, organization, validation and documentation of data to build a database.

## Must-know facts
- **Initial assessment:** done within a set time after admission; creates the database for problem identification and future comparison.
- **Problem-focused assessment:** ongoing, about one specific problem; example from the handout: checking hydration status every 15 minutes.
- **Emergency assessment:** during a physiologic or psychologic crisis; finds life-threatening problems and overlooked ones. Frame with ABC (airway, breathing, circulation) or Maslow.
- **Time-lapsed assessment:** several months after the first one; compares current status with baseline.
- After collecting: organize (cluster facts), validate (double-check accuracy), and document everything.

## Priority nursing actions
Airway before breathing before circulation, because lack of oxygen kills fastest. Validate odd data (re-measure a strange blood pressure) before acting on it.

## How the exam asks about it
Identify the type from the purpose: crisis -> emergency; baseline -> initial; compare with baseline later -> time-lapsed; focus on one issue -> problem-focused.

## Related topics
[[Nursing Process Phase 1: Assessment Methods and Types]], [[Interviewing in Assessment: Directive, Non-directive and Stages]], [[Nursing Process Phase 2: Nursing Diagnosis]]

title: Nursing Diagnosis Formats: Two-part, PES, One-part and Types
body:
## What it is
The second phase of the nursing process names the client's health problem. The handout lists statement formats and five diagnosis types.

## Must-know facts
- **Two-part:** problem + etiology joined by "related to". Example: constipation related to prolonged laxative use.
- **Three-part (PES):** problem, etiology, signs and symptoms ("as manifested by").
- **One-part:** NANDA label only, such as rape-trauma syndrome or anticipatory grieving.
- **Collaborative problems:** begin with "Potential complication", for example potential complication of head injury: increased intracranial pressure; these need physician and nurse together.
- NANDA defines, refines and promotes a standard nursing diagnosis taxonomy.
- Types: actual (problem is present, based on signs and symptoms; ineffective breathing pattern); risk (problem likely unless the nurse acts; risk for infection); wellness (readiness for enhancement, e.g. readiness for enhanced family coping); possible (evidence incomplete); syndrome (a cluster, e.g. risk for disuse syndrome).
- Activities: cluster data, compare with norms, find gaps and inconsistencies, name problems, risks and strengths.

## How the exam asks about it
Spot the correctly written statement: etiology must be something the nurse can treat; do not use a medical diagnosis as the "related to" part. "Risk for" statements have no signs and symptoms.

## Memory aid
PES = Problem, Etiology, Signs.

## Related topics
[[Nursing Process Phase 2: Nursing Diagnosis]], [[Nursing Process Phase 3: Planning and Goal Setting]], [[Nursing Process Phase 1: Assessment Methods and Types]]

title: Planning: Priorities, CSMART Goals and Care Plan Writing Rules
body:
## What it is
Planning is a deliberate decision-making phase that sets goals (criteria for evaluation) stated in behavioural terms, with the client and family involved.

## Must-know facts
- Types of planning: initial (by the nurse who admits), ongoing (every nurse, e.g. start of each shift), discharge (begins at first client contact).
- Planning process: set priorities, set client goals/outcomes, select interventions, write individualized interventions on the care plan.
- CSMART goal: Client-centered, Specific, Measurable, Attainable, Realistic, Time-bound.
- Care plan writing guidelines: date and sign; use category headings; use approved symbols and key words; be specific; refer to procedure books instead of writing every step; include client preferences; include prevention and health maintenance; include ongoing assessment; include collaboration; include discharge and home care plans.

## Priority nursing actions
Rank problems with ABC and Maslow: airway and breathing before pain, pain before education. Involve the client so goals are realistic.

## How the exam asks about it
Pick the best-written goal: "client will walk 10 meters with a walker by Friday" beats "client will improve mobility". The goal is about the client, not the nurse's action.

## Related topics
[[Nursing Process Phase 3: Planning and Goal Setting]], [[Nursing Process Phases 4 and 5: Implementation and Evaluation Types]], [[Nursing Diagnosis Formats: Two-part, PES, One-part and Types]]
outlineRefs: Guidelines for Writing Nursing Care Plans

title: Implementation Requirements and Evaluation Outcomes
body:
## What it is
Phase 4 puts the plan into action; phase 5 checks whether it worked.

## Must-know facts
- Implementation includes reassessing before acting, deciding if help is needed, doing the interventions, supervising delegated care, and documenting.
- Requirements: adequate knowledge, technical skills, communication skills, therapeutic use of self, right attitude.
- Evaluation: collect and compare data, relate nursing actions to outcomes, draw conclusions, then continue, modify or end the care plan.
- Types: ongoing (formative) during or right after an intervention for on-the-spot changes; intermittent at set times to show progress; terminal (summative) at or before discharge.
- Goal result: met, partially met, or not met. If partly met or not met: either revise the plan, or keep it because the client only needs more time.

## Priority nursing actions
Reassess first: a stable client yesterday may be unstable today. If the goal was not met, re-assess before changing the plan, because the data may be wrong.

## How the exam asks about it
"Before giving the intervention the nurse should" -> reassess. "Goal partially met" -> revise or allow more time, not discontinue.

## Related topics
[[Nursing Process Phases 4 and 5: Implementation and Evaluation Types]], [[Planning: Priorities, CSMART Goals and Care Plan Writing Rules]], [[The Nursing Process: Purposes and Characteristics]]

title: Definitions of Health, Illness, Disease and Homeostasis
body:
## What it is
Basic definitions that anchor many questions in the health and illness unit.

## Must-know facts
- **Health (WHO):** complete physical, mental and social well-being, not just the absence of disease or infirmity.
- **Health (dynamic view):** ability to keep homeostasis, a dynamic equilibrium; regulated by negative feedback (Walter Cannon).
- **Illness:** a state where physical, emotional, intellectual, social, developmental or spiritual functioning is lowered compared with previous experience; it is personal.
- **Disease:** a change in body function that reduces capacity or shortens life; it is diagnosed.
- Smith's four models: clinical (no signs and symptoms), role performance (able to do one's work), adaptive (coping; disease = failed adaptation), eudaimonistic (actualization of potential).
- Travis wellness continuum: high-level wellness to premature death; moving toward wellness takes awareness, education, growth.

## How to reason about it
You can have an illness without a diagnosed disease (feeling unwell, nothing found) and disease without illness (silent high blood pressure). The exam tests this difference.

## Related topics
[[Health and Illness Models: Travis, Health Belief and Smith]], [[Agent-Host-Environment Model and Causes of Disease]], [[Homeostasis, Negative Feedback and Cannon's Responses]]

title: Homeostasis, Negative Feedback and Cannon's Responses
body:
## What it is
Homeostasis is a state of dynamic balance. It is regulated by negative feedback: a change triggers a response that pushes the body back toward its set point. The handout notes it is now often described as "hemodynamics" because it constantly changes.

## Must-know facts
- Walter Cannon: homeostasis and the fight-or-flight response.
- Three responses listed: sympatho-adreno-medullary (fight or flight), adrenocortical, neurohypophyseal.
- Selye's General Adaptation Syndrome (whole body) versus Local Adaptation Syndrome (one organ or body part, e.g. inflammation, backache, headache, diarrhea).
- Stress sources: internal (depression in cancer), external (death in family), developmental (predictable, e.g. starting a job), situational (unpredictable, positive or negative: marriage, divorce, birth).

## How to reason about it
Cause -> finding -> priority: a stressor activates the sympathetic system, so expect fast pulse, fast breathing and high blood pressure; the nurse lowers the stressor and monitors vital signs. The trap is calling a positive event non-stressful: good change is still a stressor.

## Related topics
[[Stress and the General Adaptation Syndrome]], [[Homeostasis and the Inflammatory Response]], [[Definitions of Health, Illness, Disease and Homeostasis]]

## Check against your textbook
The handout's wording on the three phases of Selye's response is muddled (alarm, shock, counter-shock); confirm the order in your textbook.

title: Cellular Events of Inflammation: Margination to Phagocytosis
body:
## What it is
Inflammation mobilizes specific and non-specific defences after tissue injury or infection.

## Must-know facts
- Purposes: localize the injury, protect tissue, prepare it for repair.
- Cells: neutrophils arrive first; monocytes do phagocytosis in chronic injury; lymphocytes handle immune responses.
- Sequence of events:
  1. Margination (pavementation): phagocytes line up along the vessel wall.
  2. Emigration (diapedesis): phagocytes squeeze out of the vessel.
  3. Chemotaxis: injured tissue releases substances that pull phagocytes in.
  4. Phagocytosis: phagocytes swallow and destroy the invader.
- Exudate: fluid that left the vessels, dead phagocytes and tissue cells. Fibrinogen turns to fibrin, with thromboplastin and platelets forming a mesh that walls off the area. Lymphatic drainage clears the exudate.
- After this comes repair by regeneration or scar.

## Complications and red flags
Spreading redness, pus, fever or increasing pain mean the barrier failed: possible infection.

## How the exam asks about it
Put the events in order, or choose which cell comes first (neutrophil). Chemotaxis = attraction.

## Memory aid
M-E-C-P: Margination, Emigration, Chemotaxis, Phagocytosis.

## Related topics
[[Homeostasis and the Inflammatory Response]], [[Wound Healing: Regeneration, Scar and Intentions]], [[Stress and the General Adaptation Syndrome]]

title: Types of Fever and Factors Affecting Body Temperature
body:
## What it is
Body temperature is the balance between heat produced and heat lost. Core temperature is deep tissue; surface temperature is skin, subcutaneous tissue and fat and shifts with the environment.

## Must-know facts
- Heat loss: radiation (no contact), conduction (direct contact), convection (air currents), evaporation (moisture from skin and respiratory tract).
- Factors: age, time of day (highest roughly 4-6 pm, lowest roughly 4-6 am), exercise, hormones (progesterone raises temperature), stress, environment.
- Terms: pyrexia, hyperthermia and fever = above usual range; hyperpyrexia = 41 C (105.8 F) and above; hypothermia = core temperature below normal limit (too much heat loss, too little production, or impaired hypothalamus).
- Fever patterns:
  - Intermittent: swings between fever and normal/subnormal at regular intervals.
  - Remittent: swings of more than 2 C over 24 hours, always above normal.
  - Relapsing: a few febrile days alternate with 1-2 normal days.
  - Constant: little change but always above normal.
  - Spike (staircase wording in handout): jumps rapidly to a fever level from normal and returns to normal within hours.

## Priority nursing actions
Treat the cause; remove extra covers; fluids; measure again; watch for seizures in children. Do not use alcohol rubs.

## How the exam asks about it
Match the pattern: never drops to normal = constant or remittent (remittent swings more than 2 C); returns to normal between = intermittent.

## Related topics
[[Body Temperature: Heat Loss, Fever and Hypothermia]], [[Tepid Sponge Bath for Fever]], [[Measuring Temperature by Site and Converting Scales]]

title: Taking Temperature: Oral, Rectal, Axillary and Tympanic Technique
body:
## What it is
Step-level details for each site, with the contraindications the exam uses.

## Must-know facts
- **Oral** (most convenient): wait 30 minutes after hot or cold drinks, food or smoking; place bulb beside the frenulum; keep 2-3 minutes; normal 36 to 37.5 C. Avoid with oral lesions or surgery, dyspnea, cough, nausea and vomiting, oro-nasal pack, NG or ET tube, seizure-prone, very young, unconscious, restless, confused clients.
- **Rectal** (very accurate): avoid with anal or rectal disease or surgery, diarrhea, quadriplegia and myocardial infarction. Gloves, lateral or Sim's position, lubricate, slow deep breath, never force; insert about 15 cm (6 in) adult and 11 cm child as written in the handout; hold 2 minutes; normal 36 to 37.8 C.
- **Axillary** (safest, non-invasive): pat dry (rubbing raises skin temperature), bulb in center of axilla, arm across chest, leave 9 minutes.
- **Tympanic** (core estimate): adult pull pinna back and up; child under 3 pull straight back and slightly down; child over 3 on adult's lap, back and up; aim toward eardrum, insert snugly with circular motion.
- Conversion: C = 5/9 (F - 32); F = (C x 9/5) + 32.

## Priority nursing actions
Choose the site the client can safely tolerate: unconscious and unsafe for oral -> axillary or tympanic.

## Check against your textbook
Rectal insertion depth in the handout (15 cm) is unusually large; standard texts give a few centimeters. Confirm it.

## Related topics
[[Measuring Temperature by Site and Converting Scales]], [[Body Temperature: Heat Loss, Fever and Hypothermia]], [[Tepid Sponge Bath for Fever]]

title: Cardiac Output, Pulse Sites, Pulse Scale and Pulse Deficit
body:
## What it is
The pulse is the wave of blood produced when the left ventricle contracts. Cardiac output is the volume pumped each minute (normal about 5 L/min); CO = stroke volume x heart rate.

## Must-know facts
- Normal adult rate 60-100; over 100 tachycardia; under 60 bradycardia.
- Factors: age, gender (males lower than females), exercise, fever, medications, hypovolemia, stress, position, pathology.
- Sites: temporal (radial not reachable); carotid (cardiac arrest); radial (routine); apical (infants and children up to 3 years); brachial (blood pressure and infant arrest); femoral (arrest, shock, leg circulation); popliteal (lower-leg circulation); posterior tibial and dorsalis pedis (foot circulation).
- Characteristics: rate, rhythm (irregular = dysrhythmia), volume (full and bounding, or weak and thready), arterial wall elasticity (straight, smooth, soft, pliable).
- Pulse deficit: difference between apical and radial rates.
- Scale: 0 absent; 1+ weak or thready; 2+ normal; 3+ bounding.

## Priority nursing actions
Unresponsive adult -> check carotid; infant -> brachial. A missing distal pulse after a cast or injury is urgent: report immediately (circulation).

## How the exam asks about it
Which site for infants (apical), which for cardiac arrest in adults (carotid), what is a pulse deficit (apical minus radial).

## Related topics
[[Pulse Assessment: Sites and Characteristics]], [[Blood Pressure: Determinants, Classification and Measurement]], [[Respiration Assessment and Abnormal Breathing Terms]]

title: Respiration: Ventilation, Diffusion, Perfusion and Control Centers
body:
## What it is
Breathing involves three linked processes and several control centers.

## Must-know facts
- Ventilation: air moving in and out (inhalation, exhalation). Diffusion: gas exchange across the alveolocapillary membrane from higher to lower pressure. Perfusion: blood available to carry gases, nutrients and wastes.
- Costal (thoracic) breathing uses intercostal and accessory muscles; diaphragmatic (abdominal) breathing uses the diaphragm.
- Medulla oblongata: primary respiratory center; carbon dioxide is the main chemical stimulus.
- Pons: pneumotaxic center (rhythm) and apneustic center (deep, prolonged inspiration).
- Carotid and aortic bodies: peripheral chemoreceptors sensitive to oxygen and carbon dioxide.
- Normal adult rate 12-20 per minute; assess rate, depth, rhythm and quality.
- Factors: exercise, stress, environment, altitude, medications.
- Terms: tachypnea (over 20), bradypnea (under 12), apnea, hyperventilation, hypoventilation, Cheyne-Stokes, Kussmaul, Biot (cluster), dyspnea, orthopnea, stridor, stertor, wheeze, bubbling.

## Priority nursing actions
Stridor in a client = airway emergency: call for help, keep calm, position for airway. Count respirations without telling the client (so they do not change the rate), after pulse counting.

## How the exam asks about it
Name the process that fails (diffusion at the alveolar membrane), the main stimulus of breathing (CO2), or match the pattern to its description.

## Related topics
[[Respiration Assessment and Abnormal Breathing Terms]], [[Hypoxia and Abnormal Breathing Patterns]], [[Pulse Assessment: Sites and Characteristics]]

title: Korotkoff Sounds, Blood Pressure Technique and Measurement Errors
body:
## What it is
Blood pressure is the force of blood against artery walls. Pulse pressure is systolic minus diastolic.

## Must-know facts
- Classification (handout): normal below 120 and below 80; prehypertension 120-139 or 80-89; stage 1 140-159 or 90-99; stage 2 above 160 or above 100 (older scheme).
- Korotkoff phases: 1 first faint tapping; 2 muffled swishing; 3 crisper, louder thumping; 4 muffled soft blowing; 5 silence.
- Technique: right size cuff; rest first (30 minutes after exercise, smoking or caffeine); sit or lie; arm at heart level; cuff snug about 1 inch above the antecubital space; palpate pulse first and inflate 30 mmHg above where it vanished; release 2-3 mmHg per second; deflate completely; wait 1-2 minutes before repeating.
- Determinants: heart pumping, peripheral resistance, vessel diameter (vasoconstriction raises BP), blood volume (low volume lowers BP), viscosity.
- Other factors: age, gender, exercise, medications, stress, obesity, race, time of day, disease.
- Falsely low: cuff too wide, arm above heart. Falsely high: cuff too narrow or loose, arm below heart or unsupported, insufficient rest.

## How the exam asks about it
Which error produces a false high reading (narrow cuff, arm hanging). Orthostatic hypotension is a drop in BP when sitting or standing; teach slow position changes.

## Related topics
[[Blood Pressure: Determinants, Classification and Measurement]], [[Pulse Assessment: Sites and Characteristics]], [[Antihypertensive Drugs: Pharmacology Summary]]

## Check against your textbook
Current guidelines use different category cut-offs than the handout's table.

title: Abdominal and Regional Examination: Sequence and Special Rules
body:
## What it is
Rules that change the usual order of physical examination and the position for each body region.

## Must-know facts
- Exam goes head to toe (cephalocaudal). Prepare the client physically and psychologically; this is the most important consideration. Protect privacy.
- General order: inspection, palpation, percussion, auscultation (IPPA).
- Abdomen order: inspection, auscultation, percussion, palpation (IAPePa), because touching can change bowel sounds.
- Light palpation comes before deep palpation; palpate the painful quadrant last.
- Do not palpate the abdomen in clients with liver or kidney tumor.
- Flex the knees to relax abdominal muscles.
- Quadrant order in the handout: right lower, right upper, left upper, left lower.
- Best position for the chest: sitting upright; for the back: standing.
- Palpate neck nodes or thyroid from behind the client.
- Ophthalmoscopy: darken the room.
- A male examiner with a female client needs a female nurse present.

## Priority nursing actions
Safety and dignity first: explain, drape, ensure privacy, then examine.

## How the exam asks about it
Choose the right sequence for the abdomen, or the first thing to do before examination (explain and prepare the client).

## Memory aid
IPPA for most areas; the abdomen swaps: I-A-P-P (look, listen, tap, touch).

## Related topics
[[Physical Examination: Techniques, Sequence and Privacy]], [[Examination Positions]], [[Percussion Sounds and Normal Breath Sounds]]

title: Primary and Secondary Skin Lesions: Definitions and Examples
body:
## What it is
A lesion list for describing skin findings during assessment.

## Must-know facts
Primary lesions (the first change):
- Macule: flat color change under 1 cm (freckle). Patch: same but over 1 cm (port-wine stain).
- Papule: raised under 0.5 cm (nevus, acne). Plaque: raised over 0.5 cm.
- Nodule: solid mass into the dermis. Tumor: solid mass larger than a nodule.
- Vesicle: fluid or blood blister under 1 cm (chickenpox). Bulla: large fluid-filled sac. Pustule: vesicle or bulla filled with pus.
- Wheal: raised localized edema. Cyst: thick-walled sac with fluid or semisolid. Telangiectasia: dilated capillary with fine purplish lines. Petechiae: pinpoint red spots.
Secondary lesions (later change):
- Scale: thickened cells that flake. Crust: dried serum or pus. Erosion: loss of all or part of epidermis. Excoriation: scratch-like loss exposing dermis. Atrophy: thinning of epidermis. Scar: connective tissue. Ulcer: crater into dermis or deeper.
Other terms: hyperhidrosis (too much sweat), bromhidrosis (foul-smelling sweat), vitiligo (pale patches from melanocyte loss).

## How the exam asks about it
Match the name to the size or content: bigger flat = patch; bigger raised = plaque; pus = pustule.

## Related topics
[[Common Skin Problems and Skin Lesion Types]], [[Pressure Ulcer Risk Factors and Stages]], [[Bed Bath Guidelines]]

title: Abrasion, Dry Skin, Acne and Erythema: Care Points
body:
## What it is
Everyday skin problems from the skin-care section and what the nurse does for each.

## Must-know facts
- Abrasion: scraped superficial layers, red with oozing or bleeding; keep clean and dry.
- Excessive dryness: scaly, rough; raise oral fluids; moisturizer; avoid alcohol-based products.
- Acne: inflammation of sebaceous glands; limit fatty foods, reduce stress, and do not pick or squeeze pimples.
- Erythema: redness from rash, sun or fever; wash thoroughly; antiseptic spray or lotion for itch (per handout).
- Hyperhidrosis, bromhidrosis, and vitiligo are described alongside.

## Priority nursing actions
Protect skin integrity: clean, dry, moisturized, free from pressure and friction. Assess reddened areas over bony prominences because they may be early pressure injury.

## How the exam asks about it
Teaching items: avoid alcohol on dry skin; do not squeeze acne.

## Related topics
[[Common Skin Problems and Skin Lesion Types]], [[Pressure Ulcer Prevention and Treatment]], [[Primary and Secondary Skin Lesions: Definitions and Examples]]

## Check against your textbook
Dietary advice for acne is weak in current evidence; treat as handout teaching.

title: Bed Bath: Washing Order, Water Temperature and Safety Points
body:
## What it is
A step-order list for a complete bed bath with the reasons behind each choice.

## Must-know facts
- Purposes: remove microorganisms, secretions and dead cells; improve circulation; relax; prevent odor and raise self-esteem; assess the skin; provide gentle exercise.
- Preparation: explain, give privacy, turn off fan or air conditioning to avoid chilling, offer toileting first, bed flat if allowed, client to one side, remove gown and cover with a bath blanket.
- Water: warm, handout gives 110-115 F in one place and 43-46 C in another; test with the inner wrist or elbow.
- Order: eyes (inner to outer canthus, clean cloth corner per eye, water only), face, ears, neck, far arm, near arm, hands, chest and abdomen, far leg, near leg, feet, back and buttocks, perineum last.
- Wash, rinse and dry one part at a time, long firm strokes from distal to proximal, rinse soap well, lotion if wanted, change gown, remake bed, clean equipment, document.

## Priority nursing actions
Clean to dirty: perineum last to avoid spreading organisms to cleaner areas. Prevent chilling and protect privacy.

## How the exam asks about it
Which body part is washed last (perineum), or why distal-to-proximal (promotes venous return).

## Related topics
[[Bed Bath Guidelines]], [[Pressure Ulcer Prevention and Treatment]], [[Common Skin Problems and Skin Lesion Types]]

## Check against your textbook
The two temperatures conflict (110-115 F is about 43-46 C, so they agree) but are above typical comfort teaching; confirm the safe range.

title: Preventing Pressure Ulcers: Nutrition, Fluids, Skin and Positioning
body:
## What it is
Prevention steps from the handout; the page ends partway through this list, so only the first items are present.

## Must-know facts
- Provide adequate, balanced nutrition.
- Assist the client to take at least 2500 mL of fluid daily unless contraindicated.
- Give enough protein, vitamins A, B1, B5 and C, and zinc.
- Linked risks: friction, shearing, immobility, incontinence, poor sensation, heat, age, chronic illness.

## Priority nursing actions
Reduce pressure first (turn and reposition regularly, keep skin dry, lift rather than drag), then feed and hydrate. Inspect bony prominences every shift.

## How the exam asks about it
Choose the best prevention measure: repositioning, clean dry skin, nutrition. Avoid massaging reddened areas over bony prominences.

## Related topics
[[Pressure Ulcer Prevention and Treatment]], [[Pressure Ulcer Risk Factors and Stages]], [[Bed Bath Guidelines]]

## Check against your textbook

title: Verbal and Non-verbal Communication, Components and Characteristics
body:
## What it is
Communication is an exchange of information, ideas and feelings; meaning is carried by words and also by body action.

## Must-know facts
- Verbal: spoken or written words. Non-verbal: gestures, facial expression, posture and gait, body movement, appearance, eye contact, tone of voice.
- Components: sender (encodes and sends), message, receiver (decodes), channel (visual, auditory, tactile), response/feedback.
- Characteristics: simplicity, pace and intonation, clarity and brevity, timing and relevance, adaptability, credibility, humor (to help cope with painful situations).

## Priority nursing actions
Check feedback: ask the client to repeat or show understanding. When words and body language conflict, believe and explore the non-verbal message.

## How the exam asks about it
Identify the component from a scenario (the message returned by the client = feedback). Match the characteristic: choosing a time when the client is not in pain = timing and relevance.

## Related topics
[[Communication Process and Characteristics in Nursing]], [[Interviewing in Assessment: Directive, Non-directive and Stages]], [[Nursing Reports and Telephone Orders]]

title: Shift Report, Transfer Report, Telephone Reports and Orders
body:
## What it is
Reporting is sharing client information face to face or by phone.

## Must-know facts
- Change-of-shift report (endorsement): a quick summary of needs and care for continuity; not just reading the Kardex aloud.
- Transfer report: given when the client moves to another unit.
- Telephone report: state date and time, the name of the person giving the information, the subject, and the receiver's name and signature; the receiver reads it back.
- Telephone orders: only RNs receive them; a second RN may listen on another line; write date and time, write the full order, read it back, question anything unusual or contraindicated; the physician countersigns within the prescribed time (24 hours in the handout).

## Priority nursing actions
Read back to prevent errors. If an order looks unsafe, clarify before carrying it out.

## How the exam asks about it
Who may receive telephone orders (RN), what to do first (write and read back), what to do with an odd order (question it).

## Related topics
[[Nursing Reports and Telephone Orders]], [[Rules for Charting and Recording]], [[Medication Administration: Ten Rights and Drug Orders]]

title: Stress, Stressors and Coping: Sources and Responses
body:
## What it is
Stress is a response to change from the usual balanced state; a stressor is the event that triggers it. Everyone experiences it.

## Must-know facts
- Coping strategies, responses or mechanisms are how a person handles stress.
- Sources: internal (inside the person), external (outside), developmental (predictable life stages), situational (unpredictable, positive or negative).
- GAS stages: alarm (body alerted, fight or flight, epinephrine and cortisol released, lasts minutes to hours), resistance (adaptation; body returns toward homeostasis), exhaustion (adaptation fails; if the stressor persists the whole body can be affected, possibly death).
- LAS: single organ response.

## Priority nursing actions
Safety, then remove or reduce the stressor, teach coping, monitor vital signs (stress raises heart rate and blood pressure).

## How the exam asks about it
Classify the stressor (marriage = situational; starting a job = developmental).

## Related topics
[[Stress and the General Adaptation Syndrome]], [[Homeostasis, Negative Feedback and Cannon's Responses]], [[Stages of Illness and Risk Factors]]
